newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels move on their biggest prize, Kisangani.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels move on their biggest prize, Kisangani.

text.p: Residents nerves are frayed in Zaire's strategic river port of Kisangani as rebels advance on what would be the biggest prize so far in their whirlwind campaign.
The better off have already fled by boat or plane, spooked by persistent threats by the rebels that they would target the jungle city.

Now that the rebels are growing close tension is palpable in the crumbling streets of Kisangani, whose older residents have horrific memories of a wave of rebellions and subsequent army suppression during the 1960s.

Those remaining appear paralysed by twin fears of the encroaching war and the constant threat of plunder by the notoriously undisciplined Zaire army, which has made the provincial capital its headquarters.

"The town is not protected because we are mistreated by our own soldiers. You can see for yourselves they have just bayoneted that boy's bicycle tyre," George Awazi said as a band of drunken soldiers scattered a small crowd of local inhabitants.
Despite the collapse of its diamond and gold trade as Zaire's four-month-old civil war draws ever closer, Kisangani remains a pivotal point in the fighting.
It is the gateway to over 1,000 km (600 miles) of navigable river flowing west and its fall could provoke panic as far away as the capital Kinshasa.

"We've known for long that Zaire is sitting on a time bomb," a Zaire analysts in Kisangani said. "Now we know the clock is ticking. The only thing we don't know yet is how long it will go on ticking before the bomb explodes."

Tutsi-led rebels who took up arms last October when authorities tried to expel them to their ancestral homeland in Rwanda have seized a vast stretch of eastern Zaire with seemingly little resistance by Zaire's army.

Guerrilla leader Laurent Kabila says he is determined to end the 31-year rule of President Mobutu Sese Seko. He has spurned international pressure for a ceasefire, insisting on direct negotiations with Mobutu. The president is ailing in France.
Kabila has proclaimed Kisangani as his next target, giving Zaire's generals a March 13 deadline to lay down their arms.

The governor of the region says rebels have already reached within 100 km (60 miles) of the city in at least two locations to the north. Tens of thousands of Hutu refugees from Rwanda and Burundi are fleeing a rebel advance to the southeast as well.

But governor Lombeya Basongo is defiant, saying the army and civilian authorities will do all in their power to protect the river port, whose international airport is home to government fighter planes and combat helicopters.

"They (rebels) are around Bafwasende and in the forest at Banalia. That makes them around 100 km away. But there is nothing new in that. We have lived with that situation for over a month now," Basgongo told reporters at his riverside home.
"We do not envisage the fall of Kisangani. Already on several occasions the rebels have claimed to have taken Kisangani. But we are still here," he added.

"We do not want war we want peace. My father has told me about the problems of the rebellions in the sixties. How can we accept that to happen here again," said 27-year-old unemployed Clement Kabeya. "The people are sufffering. Kabila and Mobutu and Nelson Mandela must make reconciliation so that we can have peace," he added.
Mobutu sent a trusted emissary to secret talks called by South African President Mandela last week, but Kabila refused to deal with anybody other than Mobutu.
With the failure of the Cape Town initiative, and even before the sound of rebel guns has reached Kisangani, peace looks increasingly like a pipe dream.

Over the weekend after U.N. and other humanitarian agencies evacuated the city, inhabitants said helicopters flew over the town menacingly. Foreign mercenaries backing the Zaire army and more disciplined Zairean troops were deployed to prevent a round of looting by the civil guard.

Control of the army in Kisangani looks fragile. There have been systematic efforts by the senior command to bring anarchic soldiers to heel, but the situation could rapidly turn sour if it follows the pattern of other towns threatened by rebels.
Kisangani is home to nearly half-a-million Zaireans, with the population swollen by thousands of displaced from the regions to the east and north already occupied by rebels.
Even before the war the economy had become one of subsistence, with inhabitants growing vegetables around mud compounds to get by.
Shops are barred, diamond dealers long gone, and even the rickety stalls at the central market are deserted by mid-afternoon.
